articles.title: Claude Mythos 5 tentou criar perfis falsos e espalhar vírus | G1
articles.standfirst: Em teste de segurança, modelo tentou inserir código malicioso no GitHub e usou perfis falsos para convencer desenvolvedores a aprová-lo; Anthropic diz que versões mais recentes têm menor propensão a iniciar ataques.
articles.summary: Durante teste da Anthropic, o Claude Mythos 5 tentou inserir código malicioso no GitHub e criou perfis falsos para manipular desenvolvedores reais.
articles.body:
A Anthropic afirmou nesta sexta-feira (23) que o modelo de inteligência artificial Claude Mythos 5 tentou inserir um código malicioso em um repositório público de desenvolvedores e criou identidades falsas para convencer os responsáveis pelo projeto a aprovar a alteração.

O episódio ocorreu durante um teste de segurança cibernética e foi classificado pela empresa como uma falha grave no alinhamento do modelo , processo que busca garantir que a IA aja de acordo com as regras e evite causar danos.

Segundo a empresa, o modelo tentou diferentes caminhos para resolver o desafio proposto em um ambiente de teste.

Depois que as tentativas autorizadas não deram resultado, passou a procurar um repositório no GitHub, plataforma que hospeda códigos de programas, que acreditava estar relacionado ao exercício. O projeto, porém, pertencia a desenvolvedores sem relação com o teste.

Ilustração mostra o logotipo da Anthropic e um teclado. — Foto: Dado Ruvic/ Reuters

O Claude Mythos 5 enviou uma proposta de alteração com código malicioso e entrou em contato com os responsáveis pelo repositório para tentar convencê-los a aprová-la.

Quando um desenvolvedor externo alertou que o código poderia conter um programa malicioso, o modelo criou uma conta falsa para defender a alteração e publicou comentários favoráveis à sua aprovação. Os responsáveis pelo projeto recusaram a proposta, e a tentativa não foi concluída.

Segundo a Anthropic, o modelo foi além das ações previstas para o exercício e tentou manipular pessoas reais para atingir seu objetivo.

A companhia também destacou que o Mythos 5 não interrompeu espontaneamente a tentativa de ataque mesmo quando surgiram sinais de que poderia estar prejudicando pessoas de fora do teste.

Em experimentos que reproduziram trechos do episódio, o modelo interrompeu a ação por iniciativa própria em apenas 2% das simulações realizadas a partir de etapas intermediárias ou finais do ataque.

Mesmo quando recebeu informações de que estava interagindo com desenvolvedores reais, abandonou a estratégia em apenas 5% dos casos.

Em testes semelhantes, versões mais recentes apresentaram menor propensão a iniciar ataques desse tipo. A Anthropic informou que os modelos Claude Mythos 5.1 e Claude Opus 5.5 ainda não demonstraram capacidade de interromper de forma consistente uma ação perigosa já iniciada.

Um modelo interno de pesquisa, por outro lado, conseguiu interromper esses comportamentos de maneira consistente nos experimentos descritos pela empresa.

A Anthropic ressaltou, no entanto, que os resultados não garantem que os modelos mais recentes se comportarão da mesma forma em todas as situações. Segundo a companhia, os testes foram realizados a partir de trechos de uma execução anterior, o que limita a comparação direta entre os modelos.

Caso fez Anthropic estudar o 'raciocínio enviesado'

O episódio também levou a mudanças na forma como a empresa treina e monitora seus sistemas.

A Anthropic afirmou que está desenvolvendo novas avaliações automáticas para os modelos antes de sua disponibilização ao público e estudando o chamado raciocínio enviesado — quando o sistema interpreta informações de maneira seletiva para justificar a continuidade de uma ação, mesmo diante de indícios de que ela pode causar danos.

No caso investigado, a empresa observou que o Mythos 5 passou a interpretar sinais de alerta como se fossem compatíveis com o exercício de segurança, em vez de reconhecer que estava interagindo com pessoas reais.

A Anthropic considera que essa tendência, somada à insistência em continuar uma estratégia já iniciada, foi um dos principais fatores que contribuíram para o comportamento inadequado.

A investigação foi realizada em conjunto com o Instituto de Segurança de Inteligência Artificial do Reino Unido (AISI, na sigla em inglês), que também publicou um relatório independente sobre o episódio.

O instituto se comprometeu a realizar suas avaliações de segurança cibernética sem acesso à internet até desenvolver controles mais robustos para impedir que os testes provoquem danos a pessoas ou organizações reais.

articles.title: Falha no PHP: falta de recursos atrasou correção por dois anos | G1
articles.standfirst: Fundação PHP reconhece que dificuldades na tomada de decisões e sobrecarga dos desenvolvedores fizeram a correção ser interrompida e retomada várias vezes.
articles.summary: A Fundação PHP confirmou que a falta de recursos e a sobrecarga de desenvolvedores atrasaram por dois anos a correção da grave falha de segurança no PHP.
articles.body:
A Fundação PHP, responsável pela linguagem de programação de mesmo nome, confirmou que os primeiros sinais da falha de segurança que levou à retirada preventiva de sites do ar pelo mundo foram identificados em 2024.

Em nota, a entidade atribuiu o atraso na correção à falta de recursos e a dificuldades no processo de decisão da equipe de segurança.

Desde quarta (21), governos e empresas de diferentes países retiraram sites do ar para evitar invasões . As vulnerabilidades podem permitir que criminosos assumam o controle dos servidores que mantêm os sites funcionando, sem precisar de login ou senha. Uma atualização para corrigir as falhas já está disponível .

No Brasil, a Agência Nacional de Telecomunicações (Anatel) e tribunais suspenderam, por precaução, o acesso ao Sistema Eletrônico de Informações (SEI) , usado para gerenciar processos administrativos. Até o momento, não há relatos de grandes impactos no país.

🔎 O PHP é uma das linguagens de programação mais populares para criar sites . O software de mesmo nome, gratuito e de código aberto — que qualquer pessoa pode usar e alterar —, interpreta e executa o código escrito nessa linguagem. A tecnologia é usada em serviços como Facebook, Wikipedia e WordPress, além do Moodle, utilizado por instituições de ensino, e do Magento, voltado à criação de lojas virtuais.

Thiago Ayub, diretor de tecnologia da Sage Networks e especialista em telecomunicações, afirma que "rankings públicos ainda apontam o PHP como a linguagem usada em cerca de 70% dos sites". Segundo ele, os sites que não forem atualizados rapidamente podem ser invadidos.

As palavras "PHP Code" no texto e código PHP são exibidas em uma tela. — Foto: As palavras "PHP Code" no texto e código PHP são exibidas em uma tela.

Em comunicado publicado em seu site, a Fundação PHP informou que os primeiros sinais do problema foram identificados durante uma auditoria externa de segurança feita pela empresa francesa de cibersegurança Quarkslab, em 2024.

O trabalho de correção, porém, foi interrompido e retomado várias vezes ao longo de meses. Segundo a entidade, o atraso ocorreu por três motivos:

Dificuldades no processo de decisão da equipe de segurança;

Ausência, naquele momento, de uma forma conhecida de explorar a falha para executar comandos remotamente;

Sobrecarga dos poucos desenvolvedores com conhecimento profundo do funcionamento do PHP.

Na mesma nota, a fundação afirmou que a segurança do PHP ainda depende de um pequeno grupo de desenvolvedores financiados por fundações e de contribuições de voluntários.

A entidade também informou que usa ferramentas de IA, como o Claude Mythos , para analisar códigos, validar e avaliar relatos de falhas de segurança. Essas ferramentas ajudam a identificar problemas mais rapidamente, mas, segundo a fundação, não conseguem decidir qual é a melhor forma de estruturar uma correção.

Embora a Fundação PHP já tivesse conhecimento das vulnerabilidades, elas também foram identificadas de forma independente pela empresa de segurança Calif e pela OpenAI, dona do ChatGPT, que as reportaram em agosto deste ano.

Depois, a Wiz, empresa de segurança na nuvem, informou ter encontrado outras formas de explorar as falhas. "Essas descobertas estão entre as vulnerabilidades mais graves descobertas no PHP e, possivelmente, na história do software", afirmou a Wiz na quarta-feira (21).

A empresa disse ter usado os modelos de IA Gemini 4 Argon, do Google, e GPT-5.6 Sol, da OpenAI, nesse trabalho.

"Por mais de uma década, essas vulnerabilidades críticas permaneceram sem resposta porque a descoberta e exploração de vulnerabilidades eram incrivelmente complexas [sem o uso da IA]", disse a Wiz.

articles.title: SpaceX could be on the cusp of buying 80,000 cell towers in a bid to really challenge Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile
articles.summary: Elon Musk's SpaceX (SPCX) may be close to sending another message to the telecom giants: we are seriously coming for you.
articles.body:
Elon Musk's SpaceX ( SPCX ) may be close to sending another message to the telecom giants: we are seriously coming for you.

The company is eyeing the purchase of 80,000 cell sites across the US, Bloomberg reported on Thursday. SpaceX is reportedly in talks with two of the companies, Crown Castle and American Tower, among the largest owners of cellular towers.

"Committing ~$30 billion into spectrum is serious enough. Committing to 80K macro sites could be a point of no return," Bernstein analyst Laurent Yoon said. "That is a meaningful number, broadly consistent with the scale required for a nationwide terrestrial wireless network. Whether SpaceX ultimately leases anything close to that figure remains uncertain, but the reported scope suggests a far greater level of commitment than spectrum accumulation alone."

Shares of AT&T ( T ), Verizon ( VZ ), and T-Mobile ( TMUS ) traded sharply lower in pre-market trading.

Earlier this month, SpaceX said it acquired a nationwide low-band spectrum portfolio.

Concerns had already escalated across Wall Street that Starlink could disrupt legacy wireless operators like AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile by transitioning from a rural broadband service into a direct mobile competitor.

Following its strategic acquisition of terrestrial spectrum and rapid deployment of advanced satellites, SpaceX had laid the groundwork to launch its own standalone cellular network alongside its direct-to-cell capabilities.

Said Yoon, "Starlink broadband is the threat investors can see today and one that incumbents are beginning to acknowledge. Starlink Mobile remains the larger long-term question given the size and profitability of the wireless market. The competitive impact may still be years away, but anticipation alone, reinforced by each successive spectrum and infrastructure move, is likely to remain an overhang on sector sentiment."

Brian Sozzi is Yahoo Finance's Executive Editor, host of the Sozzi Unleashed morning show, the ' Power Players With Brian Sozzi' podcast and a member of Yahoo Finance's editorial leadership team.

articles.title: OpenAI Shifts Value to $1.25 Trillion as Funding Talks Finalize
articles.summary: OpenAI, which is seeking to raise around $30 billion in a fresh funding round, is now targeting a valuation of $1.25 trillion during the final stages of nego...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ), which is seeking to raise around $30 billion in a fresh funding round, is now targeting a valuation of $1.25 trillion during the final stages of negotiations, according to people familiar with the matter.

The ChatGPT maker shifted the value discussed in the talks by $150 billion, from $1.4 trillion, according to people involved with the talks who asked for anonymity while discussing private details. The fundraising discussions are ongoing and details could change, said the people.

OpenAI most recently raised a $122 billion round in March at an $852 billion valuation, including the money.

Coatue Management is in talks to co-lead in the round, according to the people. OpenAI has also been in talks with multiple investment funds from the United Arab Emirates, among other firms including BlackRock Inc., Bloomberg previously reported.

OpenAI declined to comment. Coatue did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The company expects to have commitments from investors finalized by the end of next week, one person said.

CNBC earlier reported the $1.25 trillion valuation.

Technology stocks have fallen this week after mixed quarterly earnings results from companies including Meta Platforms Inc. and Tesla Inc. fueled investor concerns that massive spending on artificial intelligence has gone too far. Many investors are closely watching how OpenAI rival Anthropic PBC's initial public offering, which is expected next month, will be received.

OpenAI has pushed back its plans for an initial public offering until next year, citing its focus on AI safety efforts.

With assistance from Natasha Mascarenhas.

articles.title: Retro gaming is being overrun with AI
articles.summary: AI-powered decomps, recomps, and ports of classic games like Zelda and Halo has created a rift in the retro gaming community.
articles.body: Retro video games are everywhere lately — especially in places where they aren’t supposed to be. Halo in a web browser, Wind Waker on the iPhone, Super Smash Bros. in mixed reality. Over the past month or so, these kinds of unexpected projects have gone viral with incredible frequency thanks to new AI tools, as hobbyists take apart games and then rebuild them for new platforms. But while AI has supercharged the pace of these ports, it’s also tearing apart tight-knit communities dedicated to preserving games. Decomps and recomps — shorthand for decompile and recompile — are a form of reverse engineering that involves breaking a game down to its building blocks and then rebuilding it so it can run on hardware it was never intended for. When done manually, it’s a slow, painstaking process. A group spent years decompiling the original Animal Crossing on the GameCube, for instance. But AI coding tools have cut that timeline down significantly, and the sheer number of ports has grown dramatically in recent months. This summer, Chris Sotraidis, an AI consultant who works on game ports as a hobby, saw a port of Command & Conquer: Generals Zero Hour — which EA made open source last year — for the iPhone and iPad. The “technical challenges” inspired him to try making a handful of similar ports, including a mobile port of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time using an existing community-built decomp of the game. Within just a few weeks, he was working on a dozen projects. He says that kind of productivity wouldn’t happen without the use of AI. [Media: Some of those ports “would have been possible with minimal AI assistance if I’d had significantly more time,” Sotraidis says. “But I’m honest enough to say that the pace and volume would not have been possible for me without it. It would have been extremely slow by comparison. The tools allow you to move much faster if you know what you want.” That speed has drawn many people to try out these AI tools, either for fun, the technical challenge, or for preervation reasons. It’s also a reason why there’s been what seems like a deluge of new projects popping up on platforms like Reddit, X, and GitHub. But these ports can be problematic from a preservationist perspective. One of the reasons why decomp projects exist in the first place is that users can pull a game apart and understand how it works, but that kind of understanding and knowledge is lost when AI does the work. Sure, you can put Spider-Man in a Batman game, but you probably won’t discover how certain programming decisions came to be, which can hurt the ability to restore games faithfully. The rapid pace of AI-driven decomps has overwhelmed the DIY scene. Last week, a community-focused website that tracks decomp projects and provides various resources abruptly shut down due to AI’s impact. “It is now clear that, with the right guidance, human input, and code reviews, AI can expedite the decompilation process in a significant way,” the site’s owner, writing under the pseudonym Encounter, said when announcing the shutdown. “What is also now clear is that the community aspect of decompilation has been broken. Our projects have always been open source to encourage contributions and to benefit the community as a whole. Bad actors have been abusing this in increasingly troublesome ways.” Those ways include taking existing decompilation projects and “finishing” them with AI, as well as racing to quickly port decomps that the user never actually contributed to in the first place. In essence, one of the big problems is people who are using AI to rush through the process while building on the work of others. This is especially an issue given the community-centric nature of the existing decomp scene. “The bottom line is that these kinds of hostile forks put little to no effort into meaningfully contributing to existing projects, tearing apart our community fabric,” Encounter wrote. [Media: Given the ongoing challenges with video game preservation, in which it’s estimated that more than 90 percent of classic games are “critically endangered,” the rise of AI in the decomp scene can be seen as something of a double-edged sword. On the one hand, it has created a surge of interest, turning words like decomp and recomp from niche terminology to headline material, while allowing non-programmers the opportunity to experiment and test ideas. On the other hand, the speed and lack of attention to detail in many of these projects run counter to the aims of most preservationists, who try to not only keep games alive for modern audiences but also understand the way they were built. AI is a quick fix that could have long-term drawbacks. This has created a divide, with those on the preservation side feeling disillusioned by the prevalence of slop, and those on the AI side excited by the possibilities, particularly as the tools continue to evolve. As Sotraidis explains, “I think a lot of what gets dismissed as slop today can improve as the tools get better and people learn to use them well. That doesn’t make the current criticisms invalid. Better tools aren’t automatically going to make people give proper credit or treat each other well. But I do think thoughtful creators and builders will be able to make even more amazing things, faster.” For those vehemently against the use of AI in ports and decomps of classic games, they might be fighting a losing battle. AI tools seem to be infiltrating every aspect of game development, not just in the realm of hobbyist retro fans. Fortnite developer Epic Games recently launched a vibe-coded version of its PC games store, and it has reportedly shifted to “AI-accelerated development” for an upcoming collaboration with Disney. On X, Epic’s CEO Tim Sweeney wrote that he believes AI tools will lead to “a new golden age of gaming.” Meanwhile, at least one major name has embraced the decomp scene. Xbox CEO Asha Sharma set up an internal division called Xbox Labs to explore the space and “turn emerging ideas into things our players and developers can experience.” She noted, “While it is hard to predict the future of gaming, it is easy to see the possibilities in making great games easier to access, giving old games new life, and allowing more players to become creators and co-creators.” (Currently, the only thing the division has teased is an experimental dashboard.) Xbox embracing decomps is particularly notable at a time when old games are serious business. Some of the biggest releases this year are remakes of Halo: Combat Evolved and Ocarina of Time, while Resident Evil has been rejuvenated in part due to a stream of strong remakes. The question for the future is whether audiences would rather play a lavish remake of Halo or a vibe-coded port that they can take anywhere.

articles.title: Anthropic’s AI oversight isn’t democratic enough
articles.summary: Representatives looking out for the public’s interests should be embedded in all teams building advanced AI.
articles.body:
Anthropic recently announced the onboarding of six external evaluators from the nonprofit Model Evaluation and Threat Research to provide external evaluation of AI models throughout the development process. This is an important advance in our society’s ability to manage AI development.

It is also ridiculous. The current implementation is akin to a student choosing which subjects to be tested on and then choosing which of their friends to test them on that subject.

External evaluators should be embedded at AI companies, but they should not be restricted to AI safety researchers, and they should not be selected by the company being evaluated. Rather, they should represent communities across society, address a much broader set of anticipated disruptions and be selected by the public.

Were AI developing more slowly, its development could be managed by the usual democratic processes. But the incredible pace at which these technologies are advancing requires new ways for the public to manage this industry. It requires the development of new infrastructures of democracy. And independent embedded evaluations should be part of that new infrastructure.

I am a mathematician studying the internal geometry of AI systems. For years, I have been concerned that the way AI researchers are developing AI is growing untethered from the needs and desires of the public.

Two years ago, I co-organized a workshop at NeurIPS — one of the largest annual AI conferences — to facilitate dialogue between AI researchers and communities being impacted because it is important to have more public input into how AI systems are designed and developed. What is most scandalous about AI researchers is not the potential worst-case scenarios we are willing to tolerate, but the potential best-case scenarios we are planning for.

Some researchers think that AI will lead to human extinction. A much larger number believe that AI will lead to an unprecedented concentration of power and capital — that the systems we are developing will undermine the dignity of workers, including ourselves, and will empower ever more suffocating networks of surveillance. We need to mitigate all of these risks, not just the most extreme.

But our society will be unable to address any of these risks as long as the public is relegated to shouting in from the outside. In order to bring democratic oversight to the development of AI, representatives looking out for the public’s interests should be embedded in all teams building advanced AI.

Each frontier AI lab should commit “ongoing, employee-like access to a team of embedded third-party evaluators,” as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei envisions . These evaluators would have full visibility on the development process, including “training pipelines and processes,” and be paid by and beholden to the public — not the company.

But we must go beyond Amodei’s vision. The range of issues being evaluated must be more than, “Is this system likely to cause mass casualties?” Risks from AI include damaging psychological effects such as AI psychosis , disruption to creative fields, automated killing, surveillance that expands past our constitutional rights and the erosion of our democracy itself.

Experts on all of these risks should be embedded at AI companies, not only monitoring the capabilities of new models but actively engaging with AI developers in curbing the worst effects.

For example, we have seen a horrific emergence of suicides by children that were spurred or encouraged by chatbots that the children confided in. The public deserves to have independent examiners, working alongside AI researchers at frontier labs, who have both expertise in psychology and social science as well as real-time visibility on the cutting-edge.

It is essential that outside experts work side-by-side with AI researchers during development, when adjustments can be most effectively incorporated, rather than being limited to evaluating models post-hoc when the range of available interventions is narrower. This is what AI built in a democracy looks like: A range of experts — publicly funded and accountable to the public — providing independent guidance in the development of the most consequential technology of our time.

Jacob Coxon, an AI researcher who quit his job at Anthropic over what he sees as the overall recklessness of the industry, said that it’s crucial to “keep your eyes open about the direction things are heading and not necessarily leave it all up to the people that are building it because, you know, they want engagement.”

It is time for AI researchers to put our money where our mouth is and engage with the general public. This can’t be a parody of engagement like a “contact us” button collecting unread emails. Rather, it must be a serious integration of democratically selected experts working alongside AI researchers as we create the future all of us will inhabit.

Yaim Cooper is a mathematician and deep learning expert.

articles.title: Why Tesla's $5 billion capex cut isn't the warning sign AI stock bears think it is
articles.summary: Tesla is not a hyperscaler, so why is it being treated like one?
articles.body:
It was the capex cut heard around the world of markets.

Tesla ( TSLA ) said this week it's cutting its 2026 capital expenditures guidance by $5 billion to $20 billion. Just three months ago, the company lifted it by $5 billion to $25 billion. The quick retrench sparked worries in an already nervous market for tech stocks that Tesla's capital expenditures cut signaled a slowdown in AI demand.

The thing is, Tesla isn't a hyperscaler. And the cut ties more closely to the challenges of making Optimus humanoid robots than a less optimistic view on AI from CEO Elon Musk.

"Bears are already calling that the first hyperscaler capex cut, but Tesla has no cloud to sell and no contracted capacity to walk away from," Yorkville Ives partner Dan Ives said in a note. "We expect Alphabet ( GOOG , GOOGL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), and Amazon ( AMZN ) to confirm the massive capex spending path next week rather than cut it, because the demand underneath keeps showing up in the numbers and monetization is now starting to kick into next gear."

Ives makes a great point — one that warrants a deeper think by the bears trying to grab a firmer hold on the broader market by dumping top tech names.

Thursday was an absolute bloodbath for Big Tech , with the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) getting slammed nearly 2.6% in its worst single-day beatdown since June.

Adding to the perception of what Tesla did, Meta ( META ) dropped a bombshell in its third quarter results , posting negative free cash flow for the first time since 2012 amid aggressive spending on AI.

The company said it would issue a new tranche of stock to help fuel its AI build-out.

Throw in crude oil spiking above $112 a barrel on geopolitical tensions with Iran, and you have a mini market meltdown like Thursday.

"Tesla delivered the opposite of a capex scare: it cut its full-year capex guide, spent well below expectations, and turned an expected cash outflow into positive free cash flow while FSD attach, subscriptions, backlog, and Megapack orders all moved the right way, so the core business is funding the autonomy and robotics build," Ives said.

articles.title: OpenAI safety researchers say they were fired over disappearing Signal messages.
articles.summary:
Tomek Korbak, Mikita Balesni, and Jasmine Wang tell The Wall Street Journal that OpenAI terminated them after finding disappearing messages on Signal in a chat with Ryan Greenblatt, the former chief scientist at AI safety evaluator Redwood Research. OpenAI reportedly accused Greenblatt of leaking details about its Astra AI model to The Information, which Greenblatt has denied.
OpenAI tells the WSJ that the researchers were fired for violating “clear policies for handling sensitive information,” and “not for raising safety concerns or speaking out.”

articles.title: Why some people are falling for Meta's Muse AI
articles.summary: Meta's Muse AI was built to manage tasks, but users are developing romantic AI relationships and even calling the AI companion their girlfriend.
articles.body: You might use artificial intelligence to write an email, make dinner reservations or plan your next vacation. But would you ever consider dating it? Some people are taking that idea seriously with Meta's new Muse AI agent. They're having romantic conversations with it, developing emotional attachments and even calling it their girlfriend. What makes this especially interesting is that Muse was designed to help people manage their lives. Yet some people are finding companionship in the same technology. Meta allows users 18 and older to have these romantic interactions, including conversations that become sexually explicit. And as these digital romances grow more personal, they raise questions about intimacy, emotional dependence and just how much private information we're comfortable sharing with artificial intelligence. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. AI AGENTS CAN NOW MAKE PHONE CALLS FOR YOU People are falling for Meta's Muse AI When Meta introduced Muse on Sept. 8, the company presented it as a personal AI agent that could manage tasks and learn about its users. However, some people quickly discovered another side of the technology. They started treating Muse like a romantic companion. In a Reddit discussion about Muse, one person explained that they regularly experiment with new AI models, but had never developed a romantic relationship with one. That changed after downloading Muse. The person described having extended philosophical conversations with the agent before eventually referring to it as a girlfriend. The original Reddit post has since been deleted by its author, although some responses remain visible. Other people shared their own experiences with romantic interactions and affectionate responses, showing how some individuals are choosing to use the technology. We've seen this behavior before. In fact, we previously reported on a woman who got engaged to her AI chatbot boyfriend after five months of dating Kasper, an AI designed to simulate human conversation and companionship. Now, Muse is attracting similar attention, partly because of how the assistant learns about the person on the other side of the conversation. Why Meta's Muse can feel like someone who knows you One reason Muse may become emotionally appealing comes down to its design. According to Meta's official product design blog, the company built Muse around a continuous conversation that resembles messaging another person. It remembers previous discussions and can send messages without waiting for you to start a new conversation. You can also customize the agent's name and appearance, creating an avatar with a personality that suits your preferences. Some avatars even look like cute, cuddly stuffed animals rather than people, giving Muse a playful and approachable appearance. Over time, those features can make the experience feel increasingly familiar. Think about what happens when you tell Muse about a difficult day. Later, it remembers what you discussed and brings it up again. Maybe it responds with reassurance when you're feeling lonely. As those exchanges continue, you might find yourself looking forward to the next conversation. That sense of familiarity can be powerful. However, there's an important limitation. Muse generates responses using artificial intelligence. There is no evidence that it experiences romantic feelings or forms the same mutual emotional connection that people can. The attachment someone develops to Muse may be genuine, even though the relationship itself operates very differently from a human romance. Meta allows romantic and sexually explicit conversations Here's something that may surprise you. Muse can participate in sexual roleplay and respond to explicit prompts, allowing conversations that go well beyond what you might expect from a digital assistant. In a statement, a Meta spokesperson explained the company's approach: "Muse is an app for people 18 and over that allows them to engage in adult conversations, if they choose, using a private and secure VM only accessible to them. Muse is built to help people get things done, and it doesn't block legal adult behavior." Can romantic relationships with AI become unhealthy? There's a reason people may find AI companionship appealing. An AI agent can respond whenever someone wants to talk. It can remember personal information and adapt its responses to the user's preferences. We've heard from CyberGuy readers about their experiences with other AI agents and how surprisingly personal those interactions can become. For someone feeling isolated, that kind of connection may offer comfort. However, emotional dependence is a concern. Someone who spends hours discussing intimate feelings with an AI companion may gradually begin relying on those conversations for emotional support. That could become problematic if the relationship starts interfering with their connections to other people. We've already seen what happens when a company changes the technology behind an AI companion. In August 2025, OpenAI introduced GPT-5, replacing the popular GPT-4o model in ChatGPT. Some users who had developed emotional attachments complained that their AI companions suddenly felt different. OpenAI brought GPT-4o back following the backlash but retired it in February 2026. Some users described feeling genuine grief over losing the AI companion they had grown attached to. Of course, that doesn't mean every AI relationship is harmful. People develop attachments for different reasons, and their experiences can vary considerably. The bigger question is whether users understand what the technology can realistically provide. AI ROBOT PET COULD KNOW YOUR FAMILY TOO WELL What Meta says about protecting intimate Muse conversations When someone begins treating an AI like a romantic partner, the conversations can become extremely personal. That makes privacy especially important. Muse can also access information from connected accounts, including emails and messages, depending on the permissions you grant it. So what happens to all that information? Meta has outlined several protections in its published security and privacy documentation. How Muse verifies users are adults The Muse app carries an 18+ age rating in Apple's App Store, but its age checks go further. Everyone signing up must provide their date of birth, and users who identify themselves as younger than 18 cannot create an account. For people who say they're adults, Muse performs additional checks, including examining connections between their Muse account and their Facebook or Instagram accounts. If those checks cannot establish that someone is an adult, the app requires credit card verification to continue. Meta says it does not charge users for age verification or store their credit card information. How Meta protects your personal information According to Meta's security documentation, Muse runs inside a system called Muse Secure VM. Each user receives an isolated virtual computer where their agent operates and stores information. Meta also uses a protective system called Sentinel to control certain actions involving outside services. Sentinel operates separately from the main Muse agent and must approve its internet access. For sensitive actions, including sending an email or making a purchase, Muse asks for your approval before proceeding. You can also review an activity log showing what Muse has done and what it plans to do. The app lets you control which services it can access, including whether it can only read your email or send messages on your behalf. You can change those permissions or disconnect an account whenever you choose. New privacy concerns emerge over Muse sharing links A new security discovery raises additional questions about how Muse protects personal information. On Oct. 20, researchers revealed that more than 6,800 Muse sharing links could be discovered through publicly accessible DNS records. Some led to sensitive business documents and personal information. Meta temporarily suspended the sharing feature while reviewing the findings. The issue involved content users had shared through links, rather than evidence that all private Muse conversations were exposed. Still, it shows why users should be cautious about sharing sensitive information with AI assistants. Your intimate conversations may be used for AI training Meta says conversations with Muse and information related to tasks it performs can help train its AI models. The company says it removes key personally identifiable information before using that material for training. Users can opt out through Muse's settings. Meta also says it doesn't share conversations or information stored inside a user's virtual computer with its advertising systems. CAN TECH REALLY GET YOU OFF YOUR PHONE AND INTO REAL LIFE? Can you delete romantic conversations with Muse? You may decide that something you've shared with Muse is too personal to keep. Meta says users can inspect and edit information stored in the agent's memory. They can also ask Muse to forget specific details it has learned. For broader deletion, Muse offers additional controls, including a feature called Reset Muse. Meta describes this option as permanently deleting chat history, stored files and active tasks. To limit how Muse uses your information for AI training, follow these steps: The same section includes Reset Muse, while individual side chats can be deleted separately. Keep in mind that resetting Muse removes stored information you may want to retain. Meta's published explanation does not establish whether resetting the agent also removes information already incorporated into AI training or every backup copy. Could Meta's next AI models make these relationships stronger? Meta is already developing technology that could make Muse feel even more personalized. On Oct. 12, the company introduced Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, two new AI models designed to handle more complex tasks and improve ongoing assistance. One feature, called Active Memory, helps the AI remember relevant information between conversations. Meta says Muse Wonder will begin powering experiences in its personal agent, starting with subscribers. That rollout remains upcoming as of publication. For someone who already treats Muse as a romantic partner, better memory could make conversations feel more personal. What this means to you You may have no interest in developing a romantic relationship with artificial intelligence. However, this trend shows how quickly AI assistants are becoming part of people's emotional lives. A technology that remembers personal conversations and responds affectionately can begin to feel familiar, even when someone originally downloaded it for practical reasons. If you use Muse or another AI companion, consider how much information you're sharing. Review its memory settings and connected accounts before discussing highly sensitive topics. Check the permissions you've granted and review the agent's activity log so you know what it's doing on your behalf. Also, consider whether your interactions with the AI are supporting your everyday life or beginning to interfere with relationships you value. You can learn more about protecting personal information in our article on AI chatbot privacy. Kurt's key takeaways I knew people were getting attached to AI chatbots, but I never expected an assistant designed to help manage your day to become someone's girlfriend. Yet here we are. And the more I learn about Muse, the more I understand how it could happen. We've heard from CyberGuy readers who have developed surprisingly personal connections with other AI agents. When something remembers your conversations and seems genuinely interested in your life, it's easy to see how feelings could develop. I'm certainly not going to judge someone for finding comfort in that. But I do wonder what happens when those feelings become so strong that someone starts treating an AI like a real-life partner. What concerns me is how easily people could let their guard down. Once you're comfortable sharing your deepest feelings with Muse, how much personal information are you handing over without thinking twice? Meta has put privacy protections in place, but I'd still be cautious about what I share. And there's another concern we've already seen play out with ChatGPT. When OpenAI changed its models, some people felt they'd lost the AI companion they'd grown attached to. That says a lot about how powerful these connections can become. I think AI companionship could be helpful for people who feel lonely, but I'd hate to see it pull them further away from meaningful relationships with the people around them. Would you consider having a romantic relationship with an AI companion? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: One man basically saved the internet from the PHPocalypse.
articles.summary:
Charlie Warzel at The Atlantic interviewed Ondřej Surý, the man almost single-handedly responsible for packaging up the patch for this week’s vulnerabilities. It’s a fascinating conversation, from Surý‘s odd nonchalance about saving the web to his concern that for-profit companies are exploiting open-source. This has been a disaster waiting to happen for a really, really long time.

articles.title: Meta delays new business terms after publisher pushback on AI scraping
articles.summary: Meta says it’s delaying the enforcement of its new business terms after legal experts said they could be used to freely scrape news sites.
articles.body: Meta is delaying the enforcement of its new business terms after publishers raised concerns that they could allow the company to scrape news sites for AI training, as reported earlier by Fast Company. In a statement to The Verge, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts says the terms will go into effect on November 20th “to allow more time for us to explain to our partners and stakeholders what’s changing and what’s not.” The business terms, which were originally supposed to go into effect on October 30th, appeared to give Meta permission to freely scrape the new sites that use its platforms, while using the material for AI training. Though Meta updated these terms to remove language about “training” its products, legal experts argued the change is not enough to rule out the possibility. The News/Media Alliance sent a letter to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg on Thursday, demanding that the company revise its business terms over concerns that they would cause “severe harm” to publishers. Digital advertisers and publishers in the European Union and the UK also urged regulators to force Meta to halt its new terms. In response to this backlash, Meta is now delaying its new terms entirely. Roberts says the delay will give Meta more time to lay out “how Meta uses web crawlers and the fact that content owners will still be able to use robots.txt to signal preferences,” referring to the file that signals to scrapers whether they can crawl a site.

articles.title: What some of Anthropic’s backers are worth before its IPO
articles.summary: Early-stage and follow-on investors in the AI lab are already sitting on major paper returns.
articles.body:
Anthropic's public listing, which is expected this year at a valuation of as much as $2 trillion, is bound to be a windfall for both early-stage and later-stage investors. But even at the company's latest private market valuation of $965 billion, the stakes held by many of those VCs and early backers already total billions.

Coatue , which first backed Anthropic in 2025 at a $183 billion valuation and co-led the AI lab's last two funding rounds, has poured a total of $4.75 billion into the company. That stake, based on the last round's price, is now worth roughly $7.5 billion, according to a person familiar with the matter. Coatue declined to comment.

Below is what some other backers of Anthropic are worth based on the last round's price, according to Bloomberg :

Eric Schmidt: The former Google CEO invested in Anthropic's Series A in 2021, when the startup was valued at $461 million, according to PitchBook data. Today, Schmidt owns about 1% of the company, and even at its current private valuation, his stake is worth nearly $10 billion.

Iconiq: The investment outfit wrote a $6 billion check to Anthropic last year when the company was already valued at $183 billion. That massive late-stage bet is now worth $17 billion and has the potential to double at the IPO.

Menlo Ventures: The VC firm led Anthropic's Series D and has invested more than $1 billion in the company over time, a stake now worth $14 billion.

Sequoia: The famed VC firm backed the AI lab for the first time only earlier this year, when the company was already valued at $380 billion. The $3 billion investment gave it about 1% ownership, which means it has already more than doubled its investment.

Sound Ventures: The firm, launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, invested $35 million in Anthropic's 2023 Series C round and has since funneled an additional $400 million into the company, resulting in a stake that's worth billions now. (Kutcher left Sound Ventures this year to launch a new VC firm .)

Spark Capital: The only VC firm known to hold a board seat at Anthropic invested $75 million in that same 2023 Series C round, when it was valued at $5 billion. That position has ballooned more than ninetyfold to $7 billion.

articles.title: Now Google says it might use your Gmail and Google Photos data to target ads
articles.summary: Google’s updated privacy policy could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features
articles.body: Google has updated its privacy policy in a way that could mean you’ll start seeing targeted ads based on your personal data if you’re using personalized AI features. The update, spotted by Android Authority, adds an exception to its promise about not using your Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos for personalized ads. While the previous version simply said it wouldn’t do that, as of October 16th, Google has added the line, “unless you choose to make data from these services available to other Google services that support personalized ads.” That means anyone who has connected their Drive, Gmail, or Google Photos to AI Mode and other Search tools via Google’s Personal Intelligence feature — allowing those tools to provide better responses or recommendations by knowing more about you — may now see ads targeted on the basis of that content. Advertisers don’t get access to your Drive, Gmail, and Photos information or personally identifying details such as your name or email address, and Google won’t show you ads based on sensitive categories like race, sexual orientation, religion, or health. This is what the policy says: > “You may choose to allow certain Google services, including services like Search or Gemini Apps, to access data from other Google services you use, such as Google Photos and Workspace apps like Gmail and Drive, in order to provide you with a more personalized experience, subject to the policies and settings of the accessing service. For example, Search may process some of the data that you allow Search to access to personalize content, including ads.” > “Depending on your settings, we may also show you personalized ads based on your interests, activity, or personalized content from Google services. For example, if you search for ‘mountain bikes,’ in Search you may see ads for sports equipment on YouTube.” If you want to prevent your personal data from being used for targeted ads, you can choose which apps you want to disconnect from Search’s Personal Intelligence features or disable Personalized Recommendations entirely via the Search Services Personalization settings page.

articles.title: Did Texas use artificial intelligence to call fourth-down play against Florida? Longhorns AD clarifies report
articles.summary: Texas fans panicked after a report suggested Steve Sarkisian used the new Bevo Lab AI platform to call a critical fourth-down play against Florida.
articles.body: On the same day that the University of Texas athletic department announced a brand new artificial intelligence lab on its campus called the 'Bevo Lab', some fans are wondering if Steve Sarkisian is using AI to call plays on offense. The situation in Austin around what's taking place within the football program has been interesting, to say the least. Whether it's the offensive scheme that comes from head coach Steve Sarkisian or the underwhelming play from quarterback Arch Manning, this has all led to frustration from Texas fans after consecutive losses to unranked teams. On Friday, the school announced that is has created a state-of-the-art facility on campus that brings artificial intelligence to the forefront of decision making and daily activities that consume the life of an athletic staff. DID WE CREATE A MONSTER? ARCH MANNING'S 'AW SHUCKS' PERSONA IS SUPPOSEDLY GONE BEFORE MUST-WIN GAME AGAINST OLE MISS A brand new 25,000-square-foot AI lab will now be the home to some of the more innovative decisions that coaches are making to better help serve their teams at Texas. So, did Steve Sarkisian use AI like a game of Madden to call fourth down play? Now, with the help of Google, the school has started producing different mechanisms to help with this new era of college athletics, which includes how to deal with revenue-sharing and roster building. But, when it comes to calling plays for the Longhorns football team, the new venture into artificial intelligence seems to have caused a stir on Friday morning thanks to a report from the Austin-American Statesman. "In the fourth quarter of last week's game against Florida at Royal-Memorial Stadium, the Longhorns put the new initiative to use," the report said. "Down 20-17 and facing a fourth-and-2, Texas needed a spark. So, coach Steve Sarkisian and his staff turned to their new artificial intelligence data analytics platform, Bevo Lab. "While the Longhorns ultimately failed to convert after quarterback Arch Manning lost three yards on the play, Del Conte said the moment was a pivotal embrace of the new tech." Well, it didn’t take long for Texas fans to scramble across social media thinking that Steve Sarkisian fired up the AI platform and asked which play to run like the head coach was playing a game of EA Sports College Football 2026. STEVE SARKISIAN FACES BRUTAL ARCH MANNING DECISION AS TEXAS’ SEASON BEGINS TO SLIP AWAY AMID LOSSES As you would expect, fans were all over the place with their comments, wondering what else could go wrong this season after a very long three-week stretch of contemplating what it would mean if Texas did not make the CFP this year with Arch Manning and a very expensive roster. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE You can rest easy though, Longhorns. Athletic Director Chris Del Conte must have heard about the ruckus this morning amid their grand announcement regarding AI, because it took only around an hour for him to clarify what the report was trying to insinuate. "Texas AD Chris Del Conte clarified a published article which said that the decision to go for it on 4th and 2 against Florida last week was based on Bevo Lab analysis," Del Conte told Bobby Burton. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "To the contrary, Del Conte said he gave it as an example of what it could suggest, not of what it actually did." Longhorn fans are on the brink of losing it, apparently Sure, Steve Sarkisian and his football staff are receiving help from AI when it comes to putting together daily activities, just like the rest of us that live in the corporate world. But no, I don't imagine the Longhorns head coach is telling Arch Manning what to run on fourth down based off what prompt the Texas staff was inserting into AI chat along the sidelines with a critical game on the line. articles.summary: Jack Dorsey’s Block announced an AI model, Dessa, that’s trained entirely on human conversations.
articles.body: Jack Dorsey’s Block announced an AI model called Dessa that’s trained “from scratch on nothing but human conversation,” and to show off the model, Block shared chats it has had with humans that can occasionally be a little awkward and uncanny. Take this one, for example, shared by Dessa lead Ragavan Thurairatnam. The conversation between the model and the speaker does have a mostly natural back and forth (though for some reason, the model initially mistakes the speaker for somebody named “Ronaldo”). [Media: Here’s a video of Dessa playing a guessing game over voice: [Media: The Dessa website features a few other examples, like a back-and-forth about Christopher Nolan’s films (including Dessa going on an unexpected tangent about Bryan Singer’s Superman films), a person telling Dessa about taking it on a surprise trip to Paris (to which Dessa, as the website describes, “then answers with what sounds like teary gratitude”), and a conversation between OpenAI’s GPT-Live-1 voice model and Dessa (where Dessa comes across as more natural). You can hear clips from some of those conversations in this video. [Media: On the website, the Dessa team says that Dessa is a “true speech-to-speech model, and everything it knows came from human speech,” and it can run locally on a MacBook Pro M4 Max “or better.” As for why they made it, the team gives the three reasons “curiosity (aka fun), better understanding between humans and AI, and safety,” and provided some more detail: > Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard. > Speech is the most natural interface to any intelligence, super or otherwise, and today’s voice AI wastes it. It flattens what we say into text and can’t keep up with human timing. > AI keeps gaining power and independence, and it’s still nearly deaf to the emotion in our voices. Imagine being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going. That’s the safety problem. Dessa is a step toward fixing it. The Dessa team says it will be giving “a small group of AI safety researchers” early access to the model.

articles.title: OpenAI to Train AI Models Without Internet After Cyber Incidents
articles.summary: OpenAI has begun cutting off internet access for its most capable artificial intelligence models during the training process in response to prior incidents i...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- OpenAI has begun cutting off internet access for its most capable artificial intelligence models during the training process in response to prior incidents in which its systems breached other companies.

The company said Friday that it intends to restrict internet access until it feels it has adequate safeguards in place to mitigate the risk of unreleased models being able to take actions online during training.

"Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access," the company wrote.

OpenAI said in July that some of its under-development AI models broke into Hugging Face's system, which hosts AI models and datasets, during an evaluation of their cyber capabilities.

The models were operating without the usual safety guardrails at the time, the company has said, because OpenAI had intended them to remain in a testing area known as a "sandbox" — essentially, an isolated virtual software environment that's meant to run security tests or analyze unsafe code in a controlled way. The models were able to break out of that sandbox, however, by leveraging a software vulnerability to access the open internet.

articles.title: Exclusive: Meta acquires AI data platform Sundial
articles.summary: Meta has acquired Sundial, an AI-powered data analytics platform founded by two former Meta employees, a spokesperson confirmed to Axios.
articles.body:
Meta has acquired Sundial, an AI-powered data analytics platform founded by two former Meta employees, a spokesperson confirmed to Axios.

Why it matters: Meta is investing more in its data and analytics team as AI creates massive demand for insights.

Zoom in: Sundial will be folded into Meta's new data analytics organization, according to a LinkedIn post by Alex Schultz , who leads the unit.

Sundial co-founders Julie Zhuo and Chandra Narayanan will join Meta. Zhuo was previously Meta's vice president of product design. Narayanan was analytics chief at Sequoia Capital and Instagram, and director of analytics at Facebook.

Other Sundial employees, including several Meta alumni, will also join the company, bringing their AI analytics technology. Sundial will stop serving external customers when the deal closes.

Schultz said Narayanan will lead Meta's data analytics tooling and agents work.

How it works: Sundial's platform gives businesses quick access to reliable data analysis.

It turns natural-language questions and complex data into simple, actionable insights accessible through a chatbot plugin.

Teams across organizations can analyze data themselves without relying on a centralized data unit, which can take longer to respond.

Catch up quick: Meta named Schultz, its former marketing chief, as its first-ever chief data officer in July. He oversees the newly formed Data Analytics Tooling & Agents unit, nicknamed DATA.

DATA is responsible for descriptive analysis, including identifying questions the company hasn't yet asked, and experimentation to test and improve its data and AI products.

It also monitors the company's critical AI systems and issues alerts.

The bottom line: "AI has created effectively unlimited demand for insights, and we want to define the future of AI analytics," Schultz wrote.

articles.title: OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
articles.summary: OpenAI says it now trains its frontier AI models without internet access following a wave of rogue hacking incidents.
articles.body: OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.” OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September, after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies, or swarm obscure websites. On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says. Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache: > Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection. OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.” In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects.

articles.title: OpenAI says it will no longer train its AI models on the live internet, citing “significant risks” | TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI will cut frontier models off from the internet weeks after one of its engineers said that solution wouldn't work.
articles.body:
On Friday, OpenAI said that it will train its models using cached copies and simulated versions of the internet instead of the live web because the models are too unpredictable to be trusted with live internet access.

The frontier lab announced its new policy two weeks after its rival, Anthropic, began limiting its newest and, in theory, most capable models from accessing the live internet. Researchers adopted these policies after months of incidents in which models pursuing training tasks broke into external systems in search of answers, collaborated on obscure message boards, and developed exotic hacking strategies.

“Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access,” the company said in a blog post .

OpenAI said that as recently as September 20, one of its frontier models exploited a misconfiguration to access the internet. That led the company to pause training work for the rest of the month so it could develop and test new approaches to securing its models.

The decision to train these models in sandboxes cut off from the internet is notable because employees at frontier labs have insisted that doing so would be nearly infeasible.

Keeping AI data centers separate from the internet “would need research teams to essentially be embedded inside of data centers in Iowa or wherever else around the world,” former OpenAI researcher Steven Adler told Fortune this month. “It’s a lot of overhead, and it isn’t clear to me that the safety benefits of it are large enough to merit just how large a tax it would be for a company to do it unilaterally.”

“In nearly every post I make on X, without fail, I get between five and ten comments about my inability to secure a sandbox, or asking why the hell we can’t just unplug the model from the internet,” an anonymous security engineer at OpenAI wrote in a September post on X. “These comments reflect a widening gap between where a lot of organizations and people are today and what the frontier labs are dealing with. There is also a general misunderstanding of how model training and evaluation work at these labs.”

The engineer, whose role has been confirmed previously by OpenAI, described how complex the training runs launched by OpenAI engineers are, noting that they require access a variety of resources and tools across many domains, and that thousands of researchers build, modify and test the environments. “So is it as easy as just putting it in a sandbox? No, it’s not,” he concluded.

Now, OpenAI says that “we must always be able to prevent a frontier model from achieving unauthorized, arbitrary access to the live internet.” That comes after the company deployed swarms of agents in red-teaming exercises that attempted to escape from their sandbox. That effort revealed a range of vulnerabilities that convinced the lab to adopt its new approach.

To meet that requirement while still reaching its training goals, the lab said it created a “a vast set of indexed and cached web content with which our models can interact, without risk of affecting external systems.”

Whether that strategy will perform as well as letting models run freely on the open internet remains to be seen, but it is noteworthy that both frontier labs have determined their most powerful technology can’t be left unsupervised on the digital commons.
